name: Drone Rock
about: Drone rock builds songs on a sustained tone rather than a chord sequence: one chord, or none, held under feedback, tremolo and a motorik or absent beat. It descends from La Monte Young's Theatre of Eternal Music by way of John Cale's viola in the Velvet Underground, and from the long-form German improvisers of the early 1970s. Rugby's Spacemen 3 gave it a pop shape in the late 1980s, with Loop close behind, and the 1990s underground, from Flying Saucer Attack and Bardo Pond to New Zealand's Dead C and Japan's Les Rallizes Dénudés, took it in blown-out, lo-fi directions. Earth and Boris pushed the volume toward metal, where the style now has its own branch, while Wooden Shjips, Moon Duo and Föllakzoid keep the hypnotic, repetitive end alive.

artists.name: The Velvet Underground
artists.why: John Cale's viola drone under rock

artists.name: Spacemen 3
artists.why: took drugs to make music to take drugs to

artists.name: Loop
artists.why: Croydon's heavier, motorik answer to Spacemen 3

artists.name: Tony Conrad

artists.name: Boris
artists.why: Tokyo trio spanning drone, sludge and pop

albums.title: The Velvet Underground & Nico
albums.why: Venus in Furs and Heroin introduced the sustained viola drone and the one-chord crawl to rock, and every band on this page starts here.

albums.title: Ash Ra Tempel
albums.why: Manuel Göttsching and Klaus Schulze stretch two side-long pieces from cosmic drift to free-rock eruption on the most far-out of the early Krautrock debuts.

albums.title: July 15, 1972
albums.why: Takehisa Kosugi's collective, recorded in a day for CBS/Sony, lays down the Japanese drone tradition in long, echoing improvisations for violin, electronics and voice.

albums.title: Outside the Dream Syndicate
albums.why: A minimalist violinist and a Krautrock rhythm section hold one pulse and one drone for the length of a record, the cornerstone of the whole genre.

albums.title: Metal Machine Music
albums.why: Four sides of guitar feedback that may or may not have been a joke; punishing as a listen, but its influence on noise and drone is beyond dispute.

albums.title: The Perfect Prescription
albums.why: Structured as the arc of a trip, the Rugby band's second album fixed the modern drone-rock template of tremolo, two chords and narcotic calm.

albums.title: Playing with Fire
albums.why: Pierce and Kember were barely speaking, and the split between gospel hush and Suicide-style pulse makes this their most varied and most loved album.

albums.title: A Gilded Eternity
albums.why: Robert Hampson's final Loop album is the heaviest, a monolith of fuzz and locked rhythm that points straight at Godflesh and Main.

albums.title: Spectrum
albums.why: Pete Kember's first solo record keeps the Spacemen 3 formula but thins it to harmonium, tremolo and whispered songs; slight but hypnotic.

albums.title: '77 Live
albums.why: The Tokyo cult's one widely circulated document: howling feedback over bass ostinatos for two hours, unmatched for sheer intensity.

albums.title: Harsh 70s Reality
albums.why: The Dunedin trio's double album opens with twenty minutes of Driver UFO and never resolves, a key text for the noise underground on both coasts.

albums.title: Lazer Guided Melodies
albums.why: Jason Pierce's debut after Spacemen 3 wraps the drone in strings, horns and reverb, the most beautiful record the style has produced.

albums.title: Transient Random-Noise Bursts with Announcements
albums.why: Before the lounge turn, Stereolab were a Farfisa drone band, and the eighteen-minute Jenny Ondioline is still the best thing they recorded.

albums.title: Painful
albums.why: The Hoboken trio found their mature sound by slowing down and letting organ and feedback hang, and the closing I Heard You Looking is pure drone bliss.

albums.title: Further
albums.why: David Pearce's rural psychedelia at its most refined: acoustic strumming under oceans of four-track distortion, with the songs faintly visible beneath.

albums.title: Methodrone
albums.why: Before the garage-rock pastiche, Anton Newcombe's band were British-style shoegaze droners, and the debut named for it is their most immersive.

albums.title: Amanita
albums.why: Flute, sludge-thick guitars and Isobel Sollenberger's buried vocals on the Philadelphia band's Matador debut, their definitive heavy-haze record.

albums.title: Depths
albums.why: A guitar-and-bass duo from Dearborn stretch the shoegaze palette into forty-minute ambient drifts, the record where drone rock shades into pure drone.

albums.title: Flood
albums.why: One seventy-minute piece in four movements that moves from delayed guitar ripples to crushing doom, the Tokyo trio's most patient and complete work.

albums.title: Hex; Or Printing in the Infernal Method
albums.why: Dylan Carlson's return reinvented Earth as a slow country band with baritone twang and no distortion, and started the drone-Americana strand on its own.

albums.title: Wooden Shjips
albums.why: Garage organ, one-chord bass and reverbed mumble from San Francisco, a record that made drone rock feel like a party for the first time.

albums.title: Mazes
albums.why: Ripley Johnson's side project tightens Wooden Shjips into song lengths with Suicide-style drum machines; modest ambition, reliable pleasure.

albums.title: Primitive and Deadly
albums.why: Earth's heaviest record in years brings back vocals, Mark Lanegan among them, over riffs that crawl; a strong late entry rather than a peak.

albums.title: III
albums.why: The Chilean trio's four long tracks lock bass and drums into a single trance pulse, the best of the 2010s motorik-drone revival.
